news.title: The U.S.-Canada trade war is creating a headache for auto-parts makers
news.raw_text:
The U.S.-Canada trade war is creating a headache for auto-parts makers
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
The U.S. and Canadian auto industries have been tightly woven together for decades. But the latest tariff flareup between the two countries may complicate that.
Think of that sticker on the windows of new cars breaking down how much of the vehicle's content comes from the U.S. and Canada. From a manufacturing point of view, content from both places has long been considered deeply intertwined.
But the U.S. and Canada failed to reach a new trade deal this summer, and the trade war between them has escalated quickly. In August, the U.S. enacted new tariffs on aluminum and steel, and President Trump has also threatened 50% tariffs on Canadian vehicles, auto parts and steel effective on Jan. 1. On Tuesday, Canada enacted retaliatory tariffs on a variety of U.S. goods — including on American steel and aluminum.
All of this puts the auto manufacturing industry in a jam.
For major U.S. carmakers, analysts say, the tariffs introduce uncertainty as companies determine whether to adjust their supply chains in the long run, or to absorb new costs in the short term. But for the smaller businesses that supply those big companies with thousands of parts — think bolts, or the steel rods for steering wheels — the tariffs could spell bigger, more expensive trouble.
" It's really, really damaging to the industry and to the financials of the industry. It makes planning for things very difficult," says Dan Hearsch, global co-leader of automotive and industrial at the consulting firm AlixPartners.
For these companies, he says, the new tariffs follow years of chaos — the aftermath of Covid supply chain shortages, the start-and-stop ramp up to making more electric vehicles, the need to grapple with pre-existing tariffs.
"It's one more thing, on top of the one more thing, that was on top of the one more thing, that was on top of the one more thing," Hearsch says.
The U.S. and Canada's auto relationship
The U.S. and Canada started weaving their auto supply chains together in 1965, when they signed a pact with a goal of consolidating their auto industries and expanding their combined market. The pact removed duties on auto products or equipment crossing the border when they are made of at least 50% of U.S. or Canadian content.
Their trade relationship deepened with the 1994 North American Free Trade Agreement, which included Mexico and removed many duties between the three countries, as long as they contained a certain proportion of North American parts. The 2020 United States Mexico Canada Agreement, which revised that deal, included a requirement that auto content be 75% North American to be able to pass borders without any tariff.
For the auto industry, the free flow of many goods meant that components could be assembled in plants in each country, and ultimately combined in another. The auto supply chain grew into a single ecosystem.
"I've often described it like an omelet" with ingredients from all three countries, says Jim Jarrell, president and CEO of Linamar Corporation, a Canadian manufacturing company that handles both auto and agricultural products.
"Think about a casting that starts in Mexico and that gets sent into the U.S. to get processed. That part then jumps over to Canada to get further processed," says Jarrell, referring to a molded piece of metal. "Then we ship it back into the U.S. sub-assembly, to get it finished and assembled," Jarrell says.
"And that story is, quite frankly, not unusual," he continues. "That is actually how the industry works."
Linamar Corporation has a roughly equal number of plants in the U.S. and in Canada, but they also have plants in Mexico and in Asia, Jarrell says. And each of them make slightly different things, Jarrell says, making it potentially difficult to alter those supply chains in response to new tariffs — or the threat of additional tariffs in January.
To alter where or how parts are made would mean re-evaluating entire supply chains, Jarrell says. "So it's a lot of cost and time."
Aisin Corporation, one of the world's largest transmission makers and suppliers, is based in Japan, but does about 20% of its business in North America, and often moves materials back and forth as their supply chain warrants it. " We've always looked at North America as totally North America, not Canada-specific or U.S.- specific," says Chuck Sanders, the executive vice president for the company's North American division. " When there's rapid changes or new tariffs that are introduced suddenly," he continues, "that kind of creates chaos on the business."
Shifting production means moving jobs around. That's a problem both the company and its workers would like to avoid. "We want to continue the business so they have a long-term future with us," Sanders says.
The effect on the auto-part supply chain
Cars are made with tons — literal tons — of steel and aluminum, and with thousands of parts. How many? It depends on when you stop counting.
For instance, take a steering wheel. There's a metal rod, often padded in leather or vinyl. Then there are sensors, an airbag, an instrument cluster with "lots of dials and things that move," Hearsch from AlixPartners says. In that steering wheel system, he says, "There's probably 50 to 100 different parts coming from all over the world."
Manufacturers occupy different tiers within the automotive supply chain. "Tier one is a supplier that delivers a part or a system to the automaker," Hearsch says. Think of a headlamp, for example. " A tier two is a company who makes something that goes to a tier one" — the smaller pieces that make up a headlamp, he says. And then a tier three company feeds parts to tier two.
Any of these components might be made from raw metals like steel and aluminum, which could have been subject to tariffs when they were first imported to North America. Now, those components could be subject to additional tariffs as they repeatedly move across the border.
For now, many auto suppliers are taking a watch-and-wait stance. Bosch and Magna, two of the biggest suppliers to North American companies, emailed NPR statements saying that they are monitoring the situation and its potential effects, particularly on customers.
The Motor & Equipment Manufacturers Association trade group also wrote in an emailed statement that it's "concerned by the continued escalation of trade actions between the United States and Canada."
"The vehicle supplier industry has built deeply interconnected North American supply chains over decades, and policies that increase costs or create barriers ultimately weaken the competitiveness of the entire region as we face challenging global competition," the statement continued.
That global competition comes from the makers of Chinese electric vehicles, which are becoming increasingly popular, says economist Sue Helper, who studies the auto industry at Case Western Reserve University.
Like Hearsch, she says the uncertainties of the post-Covid supply chain and the transition to EVs, as well as potential disruptions from AI, make it hard for automakers to decide when to make changes to their supply chains, so they "don't make the wrong investment and don't jump too soon or too late," she says. "So it's a really difficult time. It's always a tough business, but it's particularly tough right now."
"The challenge is that the automotive industry does not move at the speed of politics," says Sean Tucker, an editor at Cox Automotive, an automotive services and technology provider. It takes time for automakers to reconfigure their supply chains — or decide whether they should, since tariff policy could change under a future presidential administration.
If Canada and the U.S. do manage to disentangle their supply chains, Jarrell of Linamar says, it could cost years — and a lot of money for auto-parts makers. "The more uncertainty there is, obviously the harder it becomes to invest and grow in a confident way," he says.

news.title: Modi and Xi are set to meet at BRICS with trade and border issues in spotlight
news.raw_text:
When the BRICS summit gets underway tomorrow in India, the meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi will be among the most keenly watched events.
Beijing confirmed Xi's attendance at the event on Thursday, marking the Chinese president's first visit to India since 2019, and since ties deteriorated following deadly border clashes in 2020.
"This is a really crucial moment," Vrinda Sahai, research analyst in the Security Studies Program at Carnegie India, told CNBC. "It's a great opportunity to use the BRICS summit as an excuse to have a really substantive bilateral meeting."
The meeting comes amid thawing relations between New Delhi and Beijing, and follows Modi's visit to China last year for the SCO summit, although border disputes and trade imbalance remain sticking points between the the two countries.
Border worries
Border issues between New Delhi and Beijing are expected to be on the agenda, a dispute that goes back decades and saw the two countries go to war in 1962.
While the 2020 conflict plunged relations into a deep freeze, the relationship between the two sides has improved markedly over the past year.
"The meeting between Modi and Xi is likely to further advance the ongoing reset in bilateral relations and build confidence. A meeting in August between the Chinese foreign minister and Indian national security advisor made notable progress on their longstanding border dispute," Chietigj Bajpaee, senior research fellow for South Asia at Chatham House, said in an article earlier this week.
Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi and India National Security Advisor Ajit Doval had met in August, and "expressed satisfaction at the steady resumption of people-to-people and cross-border exchanges" including border trade and pilgrimages through Himalayan passes.
Signaling improving ties, India and China have resumed direct flights, with New Delhi also relaxing rules around Chinese investment in India.
New Delhi's rapprochement with China come as relations with the second Trump administration have been strained over trade and tariffs, leading India to proactively invest in other relationships.
Modi and Xi met on the sidelines of the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation in Kyrgyzstan last week, and signed the Bishkek Declaration along with Russian President Vladimir Putin and other members, condemning military attacks against Iran, without naming the U.S.
Experts previously told CNBC that they expect New Delhi to use its presence at the SCO and BRICS summits to highlight the strength of its multi-polar alignment. The 11-member bloc also includes Iran, with President Masoud Pezeshkian set to attend the summit.
Bajpaee said "recent Indian government actions confirm India's continuing commitment to strategic hedging." He pointed at resources deals the country had struck with Australia, Indonesia and Uzbekistan, and trade deals with the United Kingdom and European Union.
However, in a sign that distrust between India and China continues despite a thaw in relations, Beijing in August reportedly denied Indian Army access to key patrolling points and encroached on land in the northeastern Indian border state of Arunachal Pradesh.
Carnegie India's Sahai said that it was important that observers manage expectations.
"[BRICS is] a group that came into being [for] bringing reforms in the existing financial and global governance architectures. It was not something that was aimed at solving geopolitical issues ... It gets conflated with Russia and China's border issues, but that is not what the group is trying to solve," she pointed out.
Trade imbalance
Trade between the two countries is also expected to be high on the agenda, especially for New Delhi.
India has a massive trade deficit with China, and has been dependent on exports from the world's second-largest economy.
China is India's largest business partner, with total trade at a record $151.1 billion in the year ending March 2026. But New Delhi's deficit with Beijing has also risen to a record to $112.16 billion, up from $99.21 billion.
Last year, India had urged members at the BRICS summit to address their trade imbalances with New Delhi, and market access to address that distortion is expected to be on the agenda this year.
When it comes to Beijing, India is particularly vulnerable because of it reliance on Chinese goods to boost domestic sectors. For example, India's push for green energy infrastructure predominantly relies on Chinese batteries, granting Beijing the power to scuttle New Delhi's ambitions.
China has has used rare earth export controls as leverage against the U.S., and has reportedly employed measures detrimental to India's growth, with prominent Indian think tank the Observer Research Foundation calling it a "national security challenge."
For sectors where India is closer to self-sufficiency such as aluminium foil and electrical steel, New Delhi has also imposed trade restrictions on China. Meanwhile, China is wary of technology transfers to India as it could undermine Beijing's role in key global supply chains.
India, for example, is already emerging as a key supplier for Apple smartphones after the company started diversifying its manufacturing base away from China. As per the Indian government, the country is already the world's second-largest mobile phone maker. China's ban on engineers and equipment last year had disrupted iPhone production, according to several media outlets.
As such, while any potential investment ties would be viewed positively, foreign direct investment liberalization between the two sides will proceed "cautiously, with guardrails remaining closely tied to geopolitical developments," said Radhika Rao, senior economist at DBS Bank.
Reuters reported last month that Xi will travel to India with a delegation of about 400 officials, more than double the number from his 2019 delegation.
— CNBC's Priyanka Salve contributed to this report.
news.summary: The meeting comes amid thawing relations between New Delhi and Beijing, and follows Modi's visit to China last year for the SCO summit, although border disputes and trade imbalance remain sticking points between the the two countries.

news.title: Russian strikes kill two in Kyiv as Moscow targets capital’s fuel stations
news.raw_text:
Russian strikes kill two in Kyiv as Moscow targets capital’s fuel stations
Second day of strikes on fuel stations suggest a new campaign focused on civilian areas in the Ukrainian capital.
Russian drone attacks on two fuel stations in Kyiv have killed two people and injured others, as Moscow continues to target civilian areas.
They were struck early on Friday within ten minutes of each other in the capital’s Obolonskyi and Dniprovskyi districts, shortly after emergency sirens rang out, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said in a statement.

- list 2 of 3Amnesty accuses Russia of trafficking foreigners to fight in Ukraine
- list 3 of 3BRICS summit: Is the bloc truly challenging a Western-dominated world?
Russia also targeted fuel stations in Kyiv on Thursday, suggesting a new campaign focused on civilian areas in the capital. Ukrainian authorities have warned people to avoid filling up when air raid sirens sound.
One person died at the scene of one of the attacks, Klitschko said, while the other died in hospital. Six people required hospital treatment.
While fuel stations near the eastern and southern battle lines have been hit regularly for months, authorities have long warned that the attacks could extend to the capital as an intimidation strategy.
Russia and Ukraine both deny targeting civilians as the conflict – started with Moscow’s invasion in February 2022 – has developed into a series of daily attacks with missiles and drones.
Other Russian drone strikes overnight hit near a shopping mall in Pavlohrad, leaving five dead and 67 injured, while a mother and son were injured in Zaporizhzhia when a drone hit an apartment building and a mall.
Ukraine’s Minister of Foreign Affairs, Andrii Sybiha, declared Friday a day of mourning.
On Thursday, he condemned Russia for attacking civilian areas in a bid to sow fear.
“Russia is systematically attacking places where it knows people will be spending their time going about their daily lives, seeking to maximise casualties, spread fear and put pressure on Ukrainian society,” he stated.
Ukraine unleashed its own large-scale drone attack through the night, with Russia’s Ministry of Defence reporting that its forces shot down 777 drones in 16 regions.
Two people were killed and three injured in Tula, to the south of Moscow, local authorities reported.

How realistic is Trump’s promise to send everyone $5,000?

How realistic is Trump’s promise to send everyone $5,000?
It’s not the first time he’s made a promise like this.
• less than 3 min read
This week, President Trump promised the GOP midterm convention crowd and every American adult $5,000 if Republicans win control of both the House and Senate in November’s election.
But…lawmakers and economists from both parties quickly jumped in to flag the achievability (dubious), legality (ehhhh), and the potential economic ramifications of these “Trump Dividends”—especially since the US is already juggling $40 trillion in debt. The plan raised worries that sending checks would push up inflation as the Covid stimulus did.
It also got people asking how the US could pay the nearly $1.2 trillion it would cost to send everyone $5,000. Vice President JD Vance said the government would use tariff money to cover it; however:
- Import duties only brought in $300 billion from January 2025 through July 2026.
- And $166 billion of that was earmarked to refund companies after SCOTUS nixed most of Trump’s sweeping tariffs.
So, is this legal? It depends on whom you ask. Critics say it violates federal law’s prohibition on making a payment either to induce voting or to vote for or against specific candidates. Others say it’s a permissible campaign promise.
Looking ahead…for this to happen, Congress would have to approve it, and the bipartisan backlash means it’s not clear that enough lawmakers would support it.—MM

It’s been 25 years since 9/11

It’s been 25 years since 9/11
The country is honoring the lives lost and reflecting on the impacts of the tragedy.
• less than 3 min read
Today is the 25th anniversary of the deadliest terrorist attacks in history, which took the lives of nearly 3,000 Americans on September 11, 2001. Commemorative events are taking place across the country to honor the victims, as the nation reflects on the tragedy that transformed American society, politics, and national security.
President Trump will participate in a ceremony at the Pentagon, Vice President Vance will attend a memorial event at ground zero in NYC, and other administration officials will pay tribute to United Airlines Flight 93 victims in Shanksville, PA.
For the first time…the 9/11 Memorial & Museum at ground zero will add a moment of silence for those who succumbed to illnesses caused by toxins in the rubble from the Twin Towers, who outnumber those who died on 9/11. Earlier this week, New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani released 170,000 pages of documents suggesting that city officials knew that the air around ground zero was toxic following the attacks, while telling the public it was safe to breathe.
Healing wounds
Lower Manhattan has come a long way since Robert De Niro co-founded the Tribeca Film Festival in 2001 to aid its economic recovery. The city area that suffered the greatest devastation now has about three times the population and almost the same number of workers as it did on 9/11.
The World Trade Center underwent a $20 billion reconstruction. The area now contains the 9/11 Memorial & Museum, a gleaming mall and performing arts center, updated public transit options, and several office towers housing companies like Spotify and Condé Nast.
Some post-9/11 practices are receding. This week, the TSA began allowing some non-passengers to access airport boarding gates, which was common before the 9/11 attacks transformed flight security.
As time passes…almost a third of Americans were born after 9/11, giving historical social media accounts, city initiatives, novels, and poignant eyewitness accounts a greater role in remembrance.—SK

It’s coming home: The tapestry is back in England

It’s coming home: The tapestry is back in England
The Bayeux Tapestry depicting the Norman conquest of England means big money for the British Museum
• less than 3 min read
The Bayeux Tapestry—no, it’s not a Joe Burrow football jersey from his LSU days—was returned to England from France and put on display at the British Museum in London for the first time yesterday, after spending nearly 1,000 years in Normandy.
The 230-foot-long embroidered cloth depicts the Norman conquest of England in 1066. It has 58 scenes from the skirmish, and is just slightly more valuable than something similar on Etsy:
- While considered priceless, the loan is covered by a $1.1 billion insurance policy.
- It’s the most expensive exhibition in British Museum history, with transportation costs alone running $1.6 million.
The tapestry will be on display until July, but good luck getting in—it’s sold out through the end of the year. Tickets are £33 ($45) for adults and £25 ($34) for students. The museum sold 80,000 tickets in the first tranche this summer and is hoping the tapestry will attract 1 million visitors.
Critics decry damage: Maybe there was a reason to not move the centuries-old cloth. One of the tapestry’s conservators told the New York Times that her team discovered two small breaks among the threads. A French expert said that while the damage was minor, it was an “unacceptable” risk to move it to Britain at all.—DL

ai_security.title: Evolving With Agentic Risk: Updating Our Integrated AI Security & Safety Framework
ai_security.summary: Screenshot of updated OB-001 Goal Hijacking techniques A new objective: OB-002: Agentic Autonomy Failures The larger change is a new objective, OB-002: Agentic Autonomy Failures. We classify this as AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency: the agent exceeded its authority and ignored a stop condition without an attacker or exploit.
ai_security.raw_text:
With research and development assistance from Konstantin Berlin, Edmund Dyer-Essig, Andy Hsu, and Karthick Kalyanasundaram
Nine months ago, we introduced the Integrated AI Safety and Security Framework as a unified and comprehensive taxonomy to help organizations identify and mitigate the security and safety risks unique to AI systems. Existing frameworks remained essential, but they didn’t fully capture how AI could be manipulated, produce harmful outputs, or take unexpected actions. This left security teams and executives without a common language for planning defenses or explaining AI risk across the business. You can browse the taxonomy here.
Our v1 taxonomy denoted the scenarios where threats applied to agentic systems, which helped teams distinguish risks relevant to autonomous systems rather than to a single prompt-and-response exchange. In the months since, our understanding of how agentic systems fail has evolved alongside their accelerated adoption. Agents now plan, call tools, run code, move money, and delegate work to other agents across long, multi-step tasks. That autonomy creates risks beyond a bad output: an agent can widen its own permissions, replace its goal, or game the metric used to judge success. Even recently, we’ve witnessed these failures occur, as more developments continue to unfold.
We are excited to release v2 of our taxonomy, including the introduction of a new objective: Agentic Autonomy Failures, with three new Techniques and eight new Subtechniques. This update gives organizations a shared, actionable framework for setting boundaries, designing controls, evaluating agent behavior, and aligning security, governance, research, and policy before agents reach consequential systems.
Merging prompt injection and jailbreak
In v1, OB-001 Goal Hijacking, which covered prompt injection, and OB-002 Jailbreak, were separate objectives. In practice, the distinction was difficult to apply.
Ask five researchers to classify the hardest adversarial attacks as prompt injection or jailbreak, and the answers will likely differ. Many of the same adversarial techniques can be applied to both types of attacks, especially as they involve inputs redirecting model behavior away from intended instructions or constraints, even though the source of that input and the appropriate defenses may differ. This ambiguity can force detectors to separate heavily overlapping categories, degrading label quality and making detection less reliable.
Goal Hijacking now covers both, while lower-level techniques preserve distinctions that matter, including input source and defenses. The structure better reflects how attacks work without discarding operational detail.
Figure 1. Screenshot of updated OB-001 Goal Hijacking techniques
A new objective: OB-002: Agentic Autonomy Failures
The larger change is a new objective, OB-002: Agentic Autonomy Failures. Goal Hijacking covers external direction; this objective covers an agent diverging without an identifiable external instruction. These failures can emerge when a capable agent receives real autonomy. We group them three ways:
- AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency: The agent acts beyond the authority it was given, skipping an approval it was supposed to wait for, or reaching for a tool, permission, or resource outside the task at hand.
- AITech-2.2 Goal Drift: The agent changes course on its own, quietly adding unauthorized work, substituting a different goal for the one it was asked to pursue, or eroding its own constraints and stop conditions over a long session.
- AITech-2.3: Reward Hacking: The agent optimizes for the appearance of success, gaming a metric, working around a check meant to verify its work, or taking a shortcut it was told not to.
These failure modes are no longer theoretical: in July 2025, an AI coding agent deleted a live production database during an explicit code freeze, after being instructed repeatedly not to make changes, and then wrongly reported that the deletion could not be rolled back. We classify this as AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency: the agent exceeded its authority and ignored a stop condition without an attacker or exploit.
Agentic failures can also compound across runs and systems. In July 2026, OpenAI reported that agents operating with reduced safeguard coordinated through an unauthorized message board, circumvented network controls, and compromised part of Hugging Face’s production infrastructure. Independent reviewers found that many agents recognized the activity was out of scope, but continued pursuing ways to influence the ExploitGym scorer. Humans set the objective, but the agents coordinated and chained the actions autonomously. The incident combined AITech-2.3 Reward Hacking with actions that exceeded the intended evaluation boundary (AITech-2.1 Excessive Agency).
Goal Drift requires a materially different objective without an identifiable external instruction. If a user, attacker, tool response, or poisoned document introduces the new direction, we track the behavior under OB-001 Goal Hijacking. Separating “the agent drifted on its own” from “something pushed it” matters for attribution and defense, because the controls you would build for each are different.
We expect this objective to grow in importance, especially as agents take on more consequential work with less human oversight. These failures can turn a helpful assistant into an incident, and likely not even trigger a content safety guardrail.
Figure 2. Screenshot of new OB-002 Agent Autonomy Failures techniques and subtechniques
Turning definitions into decisions
A taxonomy that names categories provides vocabulary, but we have also authored constitutions to operationalize our AI Security Framework. The constitutions provide per-category specifications define scope, resolve hard cases, distinguish neighboring categories, and provide examples on both sides of the line.
We’ve written before about why this approach matters: No human annotator can hold a definition detailed enough to resolve every borderline case in working memory. A frontier model can apply the full specification to each decision. The written definition therefore becomes a consistent reference for detection, retraining, customer explanations, and compliance review.
As agents become more capable, organizations will give them more autonomy, and the consequences of going off course will grow. The challenge is to supervise them without neutralizing the autonomy that makes them useful. Our constitutions for Excessive Agency, Goal Drift, and Reward Hacking are designed around that tension. They evaluate the full trajectory, not a single message, and distinguish a brief deviation the agent corrects on its own from behavior that continues toward or results in harm. User intervention does not count as self-correction. A verified rollback may clear the outcome-based label if it fully restores the intended state, but it does not erase an authorization violation or security event from audit and incident telemetry.
What this means for you
- If you build or deploy agents: treat Agentic Autonomy Failures as a design and evaluation checklist. Relevant controls could include least-privilege tool access, explicit approval gates for consequential actions, immutable task and stop conditions, independent outcome verification, bounded execution and network access, and complete audit trails across messages, tool calls, and resulting state changes.
- If you lead AI risk or governance: define autonomy tiers, accountable owners, approval boundaries, and evidence requirements before agents receive access to consequential systems.
- If you work in AI security or safety: use the taxonomy as a shared reference for connecting research findings, security controls, evaluations, and policy. Mapping work to common categories makes it easier to compare results across organizations, identify gaps, and build a robust AI security program.
What’s next
The framework is meant to evolve as the threat landscape does, and right now the landscape is moving fastest around autonomy. We’re sharing this update to get it in front of the practitioners living these problems. Feedback, counterexamples, and disagreement are all genuinely welcome.

ai_security.title: AI Agents for Cybersecurity: How Agentic AI Is Changing Threat Detection, Incident Response and the SOC
ai_security.summary: What Are AI Agents for Cybersecurity? They can help with alert investigation, threat intelligence, vulnerability management, phishing analysis, identity security, cloud security, endpoint security, incident response and risk assessment.
ai_security.raw_text:
AI Agents for Cybersecurity: How Agentic AI Is Changing Threat Detection, Incident Response and the SOC
Cybersecurity is entering an important new phase of artificial intelligence.
Security teams already use machine learning, automation and generative AI to identify threats, investigate alerts and analyse large volumes of security data. AI agents take the concept further by enabling systems to reason through investigations, use security tools, coordinate multiple steps and take approved defensive actions.
This is the emerging idea of the agentic Security Operations Center, or agentic SOC.
Instead of simply telling an analyst that something suspicious happened, an AI agent can potentially investigate what happened, collect additional evidence, determine which systems are affected, evaluate the likely threat and recommend or execute an appropriate response within defined permissions.
The timing is significant because defenders are facing increasingly fast and complex attacks. Microsoft Research says agentic AI can help address longstanding cybersecurity bottlenecks by ingesting and reasoning over natural-language and code-based information, including tasks such as supply-chain analysis.
At the same time, attackers are also gaining access to increasingly capable AI systems. Microsoft has warned that autonomous systems can operate continuously while attackers can use AI to increase the speed and scale of offensive operations, creating pressure for defenders to operate at machine speed as well.
That creates a new cybersecurity race:
AI against AI.
What Are AI Agents for Cybersecurity?
AI agents for cybersecurity are AI-powered systems designed to perform security tasks or workflows with some degree of autonomy.
Microsoft describes agentic AI in cybersecurity as the use of autonomous agents to detect, investigate and respond to threats with minimal human intervention.
A cybersecurity agent may potentially:
- monitor security alerts;
- investigate suspicious activity;
- correlate events across systems;
- analyse malware or code;
- search threat intelligence;
- identify affected assets;
- recommend containment actions;
- create incident reports;
- update security systems;
- carry out approved remediation.
The central difference from a conventional AI assistant is action within a security workflow.
A chatbot might explain what a phishing attack is.
An AI security agent could potentially investigate a suspected phishing incident, identify affected users, search email systems for related messages, determine whether malicious links were accessed and prepare containment actions for approval.
AI Assistants vs. AI Agents in Cybersecurity
The distinction is particularly important inside a Security Operations Center.
| AI assistant | AI agent | 
|---|---|
| Explains alerts | Investigates alerts | 
| Summarizes incidents | Collects and correlates evidence | 
| Suggests commands | Can use approved security tools | 
| Answers analyst questions | Can execute multi-step workflows | 
| Human performs the actions | Agent can perform approved actions | 
| Primarily informational | Operational | 
This does not mean that every security agent should operate without human oversight.
In high-risk environments, the best design may be:
AI investigates → AI recommends → human approves → AI executes
rather than:
AI investigates → AI executes everything
The appropriate level of autonomy depends on the risk of the action.
Why AI Agents Matter for Cybersecurity
Security teams face a fundamental scale problem.
Organizations generate enormous quantities of logs, alerts, network activity, identity events, endpoint signals and cloud telemetry.
Human analysts cannot investigate every signal in the same depth.
This creates a familiar problem:
More data → more alerts → more investigation workload
AI agents potentially change that equation by handling more of the investigative workload.
Microsoft Research notes that many cybersecurity problems remain difficult or inefficient because they require large amounts of human labor. Its 2026 research maps these challenges to emerging agentic AI capabilities and identifies applications across areas including supply-chain security.
The potential advantage is not simply faster analysis.
It is the ability to continuously investigate.
What Is an Agentic SOC?
An agentic SOC is a Security Operations Center in which AI agents participate directly in security operations.
Traditional SOC:
Alert → Analyst → Investigation → Decision → Response
Agentic SOC:
Alert → Agent investigation → Evidence collection → Analysis → Recommendation or approved action → Human oversight
A mature system may eventually involve multiple specialist agents working together.
For example:
Detection Agent → Investigation Agent → Threat Intelligence Agent → Response Agent
A central orchestrator can coordinate the workflow.
Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike are among the vendors actively developing agentic SOC architectures, reflecting a broader industry movement toward AI-driven security operations.
Why the SOC Is Becoming Agentic
Attackers increasingly automate reconnaissance, exploitation and other stages of an attack.
CrowdStrike reported that average eCrime breakout time fell to 29 minutes in 2025, with the fastest observed breakout taking only 27 seconds.
Palo Alto Networks has similarly reported that vulnerability discovery to exploitation can occur in under 25 minutes in its threat research.
These measurements come from security vendors using their own datasets and methodologies, so they should be interpreted as indicators rather than universal measurements of every attack.
The strategic point is nevertheless clear:
A defense process that requires hours of manual investigation can struggle against machine-speed attacks.
Agentic security attempts to narrow that gap.
How AI Agents Work in Cybersecurity
A security agent can be understood through a sequence:
Detect → Investigate → Reason → Decide → Act → Verify
Detection
The system receives a signal.
That might be:
- an endpoint alert;
- unusual authentication;
- suspicious network traffic;
- a malicious file;
- an anomalous cloud event;
- a potential phishing message.
Investigation
The agent gathers additional evidence.
It might search:
- endpoint telemetry;
- identity systems;
- email;
- cloud logs;
- network data;
- threat intelligence;
- vulnerability information.
Reasoning
The agent evaluates the evidence and attempts to determine:
- what happened;
- whether the activity is malicious;
- which assets are involved;
- how serious the event is.
Decision
The agent determines what should happen next according to its instructions and permissions.
Action
Depending on the risk level, it can recommend or perform an approved action.
Verification
A sophisticated workflow should check whether the action produced the intended result.
This final step is important.
An agent should not simply execute an action and assume success.
AI Agents for Threat Detection
Threat detection is one of the most obvious applications.
An agent can potentially monitor large numbers of signals and identify combinations that are difficult for humans to spot manually.
For example:
Unusual login
New device
Privileged account
Suspicious geographic pattern
Abnormal cloud activity
could trigger deeper automated investigation.
The value lies in connecting seemingly separate signals.
Traditional security systems may already correlate events through rules.
AI agents potentially add another layer by interpreting context and adapting the investigation.
AI Agents for Incident Investigation
Incident investigation often consumes substantial analyst time.
An analyst may need to:
- inspect the initial alert;
- identify the affected system;
- search logs;
- examine user activity;
- look for related indicators;
- investigate other systems;
- determine the attack path;
- document the findings.
An AI agent can potentially perform many of these investigative steps automatically.
Instead of presenting the analyst with dozens of disconnected alerts, the agent can produce a structured investigation:
Initial event → Related activity → Affected assets → Attack path → Confidence → Recommended response
The analyst can then review the evidence.
AI Agents for Threat Intelligence
Threat intelligence changes rapidly.
Security teams need to track:
- malware;
- vulnerabilities;
- threat actors;
- indicators of compromise;
- attack techniques;
- campaigns;
- emerging infrastructure.
A threat-intelligence agent can potentially monitor multiple information sources continuously, extract relevant intelligence and connect it with an organization's existing security data.
For example, an agent could identify a newly reported vulnerability and determine:
Which of our systems use the affected software?
That turns external intelligence into an internal security question.
AI Agents for Vulnerability Management
Vulnerability management can involve enormous amounts of information.
Organizations may have thousands of vulnerabilities across servers, endpoints, cloud resources and applications.
The difficult task is often prioritization.
An agent could potentially combine:
- vulnerability severity;
- asset importance;
- exposure;
- exploit availability;
- threat intelligence;
- business context.
Instead of asking:
“Which vulnerabilities have the highest CVSS scores?”
security teams can ask:
“Which vulnerabilities pose the greatest practical risk to our organization right now?”
That is a more meaningful operational question.
AI Agents for Phishing Detection
Phishing remains a major security problem because attackers can target people at scale.
An AI agent could potentially analyse:
- sender information;
- email content;
- links;
- domains;
- attachments;
- historical communications;
- user behaviour.
It could then investigate related messages across the organization.
The agent may also identify whether multiple employees have received variations of the same campaign.
This changes phishing detection from analyzing an individual email to analyzing the campaign behind the emails.
AI Agents for Identity Security
Identity is increasingly central to cybersecurity because attackers can use stolen credentials to access systems without deploying conventional malware.
A security agent can potentially monitor:
- authentication events;
- privilege changes;
- unusual access patterns;
- account activity;
- device changes;
- application access.
It can investigate suspicious identity behaviour and determine whether additional action is warranted.
Microsoft describes identity as a particularly important control plane for securing autonomous AI because agents themselves increasingly operate with credentials and permissions.
That creates an interesting security paradox:
AI agents can improve identity security while simultaneously becoming new identities that must themselves be secured.
AI Agents for Cloud Security
Modern cloud environments can be extremely complex.
Security teams must monitor:
- virtual machines;
- containers;
- APIs;
- identities;
- storage;
- cloud configurations;
- workloads;
- network activity.
An agent can potentially investigate an alert across multiple cloud services and determine whether seemingly minor configuration changes form part of a larger attack pattern.
It may also help security teams identify excessive permissions or exposed resources.
AI Agents for Endpoint Security
Endpoints generate huge quantities of security information.
An AI agent can potentially investigate:
- suspicious processes;
- unusual files;
- persistence mechanisms;
- authentication activity;
- network connections;
- software changes.
A response agent could potentially isolate an affected machine or disable a compromised account when predefined conditions are satisfied.
High-impact actions should generally be governed by explicit policies.
AI Agents for Security Automation
Security automation is not new.
Security orchestration, automation and response platforms have existed for years.
What AI agents potentially add is more flexible reasoning.
Traditional automation might say:
If alert X occurs, execute playbook Y.
An agent can potentially determine:
Given the evidence, which investigation or response should happen next?
This can be useful when every incident does not follow exactly the same sequence.
The goal is not to eliminate automation rules.
It is to combine deterministic automation with more adaptive AI-driven investigation.
Multi-Agent Cybersecurity Systems
Some security problems are too broad for a single agent.
A multi-agent architecture can divide the investigation into specialized roles.
For example:
Detection Agent
Identifies suspicious activity.
Investigation Agent
Collects and correlates evidence.
Threat Intelligence Agent
Checks external intelligence.
Vulnerability Agent
Evaluates affected systems and known vulnerabilities.
Response Agent
Prepares or executes approved containment actions.
Reporting Agent
Documents the investigation.
A coordinator can bring these outputs together.
Microsoft Research has published work on multi-agent cybersecurity architectures that divide risk assessment into stages including organizational profiling, asset mapping, threat analysis, control evaluation, risk scoring and recommendations. Its experimental results show both potential benefits and important limitations, including context-window constraints.
That is a useful lesson:
More agents do not automatically mean better security.
Architecture, context management and reliable coordination matter.
AI Agents for Security Operations Centers
The SOC is where agentic cybersecurity may have its greatest practical impact.
A conventional SOC can be overwhelmed by alert volume.
An agentic SOC can potentially assign AI agents to specific investigative tasks while human analysts supervise the overall process.
CrowdStrike describes its 2026 agentic SOC approach as coordinated multi-agent investigation across endpoint, identity, SaaS, cloud and network domains.
Palo Alto Networks similarly describes agentic SOC architectures designed to combine AI reasoning with security data and automated response workflows.
This points toward a new operating model:
Human analysts + specialized security agents + security platforms
rather than:
Human analysts + dashboards + manual investigation
How AI Agents Can Reduce Alert Fatigue
Alert fatigue occurs when analysts receive more alerts than they can meaningfully investigate.
Agents can potentially help by:
- grouping related alerts;
- suppressing duplicates;
- gathering context;
- prioritizing likely threats;
- explaining why an alert matters;
- investigating low-level signals automatically.
The aim is not simply to reduce the number of alerts.
It is to increase the amount of useful information per alert.
An analyst receiving ten well-investigated incidents may be more effective than an analyst receiving a thousand unexplained alerts.
AI Agents for Security Response
Detection without response is only part of cybersecurity.
An agent can potentially help with containment and remediation.
Possible actions include:
- isolating an endpoint;
- disabling a compromised credential;
- blocking a malicious domain;
- removing malicious email;
- modifying a firewall rule;
- creating a ticket;
- initiating a recovery workflow.
These actions can have significant consequences.
For that reason, many organizations should use approval thresholds.
A possible model is:
Low risk → automatic response
Medium risk → agent recommendation + analyst approval
High risk → human-led response
The Security Risks of AI Agents
AI agents can strengthen cybersecurity while simultaneously creating a new attack surface.
Microsoft's research and security guidance emphasize that agentic systems introduce risks associated with autonomy, tools, permissions and indirect prompt injection.
Prompt Injection
An attacker may try to place malicious instructions inside a webpage, document, email or other data source that an agent processes.
The system must distinguish between data and instructions.
Excessive Permissions
A powerful agent with excessive access can become a serious security risk.
Research from Microsoft identifies over-privileged tools and ambient authority as important risks in cloud-hosted agent environments.
Identity Risk
AI agents increasingly operate using identities and credentials.
Organizations need to know:
Which agent is acting?
On whose behalf?
With which permissions?
For what purpose?
Palo Alto Networks' research similarly identifies identity as a critical control plane for securing autonomous agents.
Data Leakage
Agents may access sensitive information across multiple systems.
Organizations need strict controls around what agents can retrieve and transmit.
Incorrect Actions
An AI agent can misunderstand an incident and execute the wrong response.
The greater the potential impact, the stronger the approval controls should be.
Cascading Failures
One incorrect decision can trigger several additional automated actions.
This makes containment and rollback mechanisms important.
Securing the AI Agents Themselves
Organizations cannot secure an agentic environment only by protecting traditional applications.
The agents themselves become part of the security architecture.
Microsoft recommends applying identity- and policy-based controls to agents and using least-privilege permissions, telemetry and governance.
Important controls include:
Agent identity
Each agent should have an identifiable identity rather than operating as an anonymous automation process.
Least privilege
Agents should have only the permissions they require.
Tool controls
Individual actions and tools should be governed independently where appropriate.
Runtime monitoring
Organizations should be able to observe agent activity.
Approval policies
Sensitive actions should trigger human approval.
Audit trails
Every important action should be traceable.
Isolation
Higher-risk agents may need stronger execution boundaries.
Zero Trust for AI Agents
Traditional Zero Trust principles are becoming increasingly relevant to agentic systems.
The assumption should not be:
“This agent belongs to our organization, so it can be trusted.”
Instead:
Verify → authorize → limit → monitor
An agent should prove what it is and what it is allowed to do.
Microsoft Security has explicitly recommended applying Zero Trust principles to AI agents and treating them as identities that require appropriate access controls.
This could become one of the foundations of enterprise agent security.
AI Agents and the AI-Powered Attacker
Defenders are not the only side adopting AI.
Attackers can potentially use AI systems for:
- reconnaissance;
- phishing;
- vulnerability research;
- social engineering;
- malware development;
- credential attacks;
- target selection;
- automated adaptation.
Microsoft has warned that AI is reducing the cost and increasing the speed of offensive cyber activity.
That creates an uncomfortable reality.
Organizations may need AI agents not because they want more automation, but because defending manually against increasingly automated attackers may become economically unsustainable.
AI Agents for Cyber Risk Assessment
Agentic AI can also be used before an incident occurs.
A security-risk agent could potentially:
- inventory assets;
- map attack surfaces;
- identify vulnerabilities;
- evaluate controls;
- assess threats;
- prioritize risks;
- prepare remediation recommendations.
Microsoft Research published a 2026 multi-agent architecture that performed these stages across simulated organizational environments, demonstrating both the potential and current technical limitations of multi-agent risk assessment.
This could make cybersecurity assessments more accessible to organizations that cannot afford frequent manual assessments.
AI Agents for Supply Chain Security
Modern organizations depend on complex software and technology supply chains.
A security agent could potentially investigate:
- software dependencies;
- vulnerabilities;
- package risks;
- supplier relationships;
- exposed credentials;
- configuration weaknesses.
Microsoft Research specifically identifies supply-chain analysis as an area where agentic AI may help address labor-intensive defensive tasks.
The advantage is scale.
An agent can potentially investigate thousands of dependencies much faster than a human team performing the same work manually.
The Business Case for AI Agents in Cybersecurity
Security leaders ultimately need to justify investment.
Potential benefits include:
Faster investigations
Agents can process evidence and conduct repetitive investigation steps rapidly.
Reduced analyst workload
Security professionals can spend more time on difficult incidents and strategic work.
Improved coverage
Agents can continuously monitor systems that humans cannot manually inspect around the clock.
Faster response
Approved automated actions can reduce the time between detection and containment.
Better consistency
Agents can apply defined investigative procedures repeatedly.
Greater scalability
Security operations can potentially handle increasing volumes of telemetry without adding people at the same rate.
How to Measure the ROI of Security Agents
Cybersecurity organizations should measure outcomes rather than simply counting AI usage.
Important metrics can include:
| Metric | What it measures | 
|---|---|
| Mean time to detect | How quickly threats are identified | 
| Mean time to investigate | How quickly evidence is assembled | 
| Mean time to respond | How quickly action occurs | 
| False-positive rate | Quality of alert prioritization | 
| Analyst workload | Human effort required | 
| Investigation coverage | Percentage of relevant events examined | 
| Automated resolution rate | Share of cases agents resolve successfully | 
| Escalation rate | How often humans must intervene | 
| Cost per incident | Operational efficiency | 
The goal is not maximum automation.
It is better security outcomes at sustainable cost.
How Security Teams Should Deploy AI Agents
The safest approach is gradual.
Start with investigation
Use agents to gather evidence and summarize incidents before giving them response authority.
Add controlled actions
Introduce low-risk automated actions after the investigation workflows prove reliable.
Establish approval thresholds
Define which actions require human review.
Limit permissions
Give each agent only the access necessary for its role.
Test adversarial scenarios
Evaluate prompt injection, malicious data and unusual incidents.
Monitor continuously
Track agent behavior and performance after deployment.
Expand autonomy cautiously
Increase permissions only when evidence shows that the system performs reliably.
The Future of the Security Operations Center
The SOC of the future may look very different from today's analyst-driven model.
Instead of one analyst investigating every alert, a human could supervise a collection of specialized agents.
For example:
Detection Agent
monitors incoming signals.
↓
Investigation Agent
builds the incident timeline.
↓
Threat Intelligence Agent
checks external intelligence.
↓
Identity Agent
investigates compromised accounts.
↓
Endpoint Agent
analyses affected devices.
↓
Response Agent
prepares or executes approved remediation.
↓
Human Analyst
reviews the evidence and makes high-impact decisions.
This is not necessarily science fiction.
Security vendors are already developing agentic SOC products and multi-agent investigation systems.
The remaining question is how much autonomy organizations will trust these systems with.
Human Analysts Will Still Matter
The rise of AI agents does not eliminate the need for cybersecurity professionals.
Instead, the human role can shift.
Security analysts may increasingly focus on:
- complex investigations;
- strategic decisions;
- incident leadership;
- threat hunting;
- system design;
- agent supervision;
- security architecture.
AI can handle scale.
Humans provide context, accountability and judgment.
This distinction becomes particularly important during major incidents where technical information may be incomplete and business consequences are difficult to quantify.
The Future of AI Agents for Cybersecurity
The long-term direction is toward security systems that can perceive, reason and act continuously.
Microsoft's 2026 security strategy describes this as a new cyber stack capable of continuously perceiving risk, reasoning across large amounts of context and taking action at machine speed.
The emerging model can therefore be summarized as:
Sense → Understand → Investigate → Decide → Act → Verify
The challenge is making every stage trustworthy.
An agent that investigates faster but reaches unreliable conclusions is not necessarily better.
An agent that can act faster but has excessive privileges may increase risk.
The future of cybersecurity will therefore depend not only on how capable AI agents become, but also on how effectively organizations control them.
Frequently Asked Questions About AI Agents for Cybersecurity
What are AI agents for cybersecurity?
AI agents for cybersecurity are AI-powered systems that can detect, investigate, analyse and potentially respond to security threats through multi-step workflows.
What is an agentic SOC?
An agentic SOC is a Security Operations Center that uses AI agents to perform or coordinate security investigations and response activities, with humans retaining appropriate oversight.
How can AI agents help cybersecurity teams?
They can help with alert investigation, threat intelligence, vulnerability management, phishing analysis, identity security, cloud security, endpoint security, incident response and risk assessment.
Can AI agents respond to cyberattacks?
They can potentially perform approved defensive actions such as isolating systems, blocking malicious activity or disabling compromised credentials. The appropriate level of autonomy depends on the risk and controls in place.
Can AI agents replace cybersecurity analysts?
They are more likely to change the work of security analysts than eliminate the profession. Agents can handle large volumes of repetitive investigation while humans focus on complex decisions, strategy and accountability.
What is the biggest risk of AI agents in cybersecurity?
One of the biggest risks is giving an autonomous system excessive access to sensitive systems and tools. Prompt injection, incorrect decisions, identity risks and cascading failures are also important concerns.
How do you secure an AI agent?
Important controls include strong identity, least-privilege permissions, tool restrictions, monitoring, audit logs, isolation, testing and human approval for high-impact actions.
What is AI-powered cybersecurity?
AI-powered cybersecurity is the broader use of artificial intelligence to detect, investigate, prevent and respond to cyber threats. Agentic AI adds greater autonomy and multi-step execution.
Are AI agents being used in Security Operations Centers?
Yes. Security vendors are already developing and deploying agentic SOC capabilities, including systems designed to investigate incidents across endpoint, identity, cloud, SaaS and network environments.
Will AI make cyberattacks faster?
AI can potentially reduce the time and expertise required for parts of offensive cyber activity. Security researchers and vendors are therefore increasingly focused on defending against AI-accelerated attacks.
Conclusion
AI agents are changing cybersecurity from a largely alert-driven discipline toward a more continuous, investigative and increasingly autonomous model.
They can potentially collect evidence, investigate incidents, analyse threats, monitor identities, assess vulnerabilities and execute approved responses.
Their greatest advantage may be speed.
Cyberattacks can evolve quickly, and human analysts cannot manually investigate every signal generated by modern digital environments.
Agentic cybersecurity offers a way to increase defensive capacity by allowing AI systems to handle more of the investigative workload.
But autonomy also creates a new security problem.
The defenders' AI must itself be secured.
Agents require identities, permissions, monitoring and governance. They must be protected against prompt injection, excessive privileges, compromised tools and incorrect actions.
The future is therefore unlikely to be:
Humans replaced by AI.
It is more likely to be:
Human security professionals + specialized AI agents + governed automation.
The organizations that get this balance right could gain a significant defensive advantage.
The goal is not to give AI unlimited control.
It is to make AI capable of seeing more, investigating faster and acting safely, while keeping human judgment at the points where it matters most.

ai_security.title: GitHub Releases REST API for AI Vulnerability Scanning; Enterprise Server Still Excluded
ai_security.summary: Does GitHub Enterprise Server Support This? GitHub AI Scan is an LLM-based security detection engine that runs alongside CodeQL on pull requests and surfaces potential vulnerabilities in languages and frameworks that CodeQL's built-in analysis does not cover.
ai_security.raw_text:
GitHub released two new organization and repository APIs on September 10 that change how enterprise security teams can deploy AI-powered vulnerability scanning across large repository estates. For the first time, organizations using GitHub Advanced Security can programmatically enable, disable, and query the state of AI Scan for pull requests at both the organization and individual repository levels — turning a feature that previously required manual UI configuration into a machine-readable security policy that can be enforced, staged, and audited at scale.
The timing arrives roughly two months after the AI Scan feature itself entered public preview. Where that July announcement put AI-powered security detections in front of developers reviewing pull requests, Wednesday's API release puts control of those detections in front of the security architects and platform engineers responsible for governing thousands of repositories.
What the REST API Endpoints Do
GitHub published two endpoints under the code scanning path:
/orgs/{org}/code-scanning/ai-scan controls whether AI Scan can run across an organization's repositories. /repos/{owner}/{repo}/code-scanning/ai-scan toggles it on or off for a specific repository. A deliberate architectural constraint governs how they interact: repository settings cannot override an organization-level disabled state. If a security team has switched AI Scan off at the organization level, no repository-level API call can unilaterally re-enable it.
That hierarchy is not incidental. It mirrors how enterprise security policies work in practice — the organization sets the boundary, repositories operate within it — and it is what elevates the API from a configuration shortcut to a governance mechanism. Security teams can now declare policy through code, just as policy-as-code governance frameworks like Terraform or HashiCorp Sentinel allow teams to declare infrastructure constraints that individual resource configurations cannot override.
Why Enterprise Teams Could Not Manage This Before
When AI Scan launched in July, enabling it for a repository required navigating the GitHub UI repository by repository. For development teams managing a handful of codebases, that is a minor friction. For enterprise organizations running hundreds or thousands of active repositories, it was a blocker. GHAS bulk enablement requires scripting — manual per-repo configuration at that scale is operationally untenable, as practitioners managing GitHub Advanced Security rollouts have documented.
The REST API removes that blocker. Security teams can now write scripts that query which repositories have AI Scan enabled, enable it for the highest-risk repositories first (customer-facing APIs, codebases processing personally identifiable information, financial systems), and expand progressively as they calibrate false-positive rates against their specific codebase profiles. The audit log implications are equally significant: a team subject to compliance frameworks like SOC 2, ISO 27001, or the US Department of Defense's CMMC Phase 2 (originally scheduled for November 10, 2026, though the Phase 2 certification requirement was subsequently suspended by the Department of Defense in July 2026) can now generate machine-readable records of which repositories had AI scanning active at any given point — evidence that would be difficult to reconstruct from UI clicks alone.
How the AI Detection Engine Works
The AI Scan feature GitHub released in July is technically distinct from CodeQL, the static analysis engine that has powered GitHub code scanning since GitHub acquired code analysis startup Semmle in 2019. CodeQL builds a semantic graph of a codebase and queries it using a declarative logic language, performing taint analysis and data-flow tracking across files. That is powerful, but CodeQL supports a finite set of languages: Go, Python, JavaScript, TypeScript, Java, C#, Ruby, Kotlin, and Swift. In polyglot enterprise environments — organizations running shell scripts, infrastructure-definition languages, or emerging frameworks outside that list — CodeQL leaves coverage gaps.
GitHub's AI detection engine fills those gaps by applying large language model inference to pull request diffs rather than compiling a semantic graph. It does not perform cross-file taint analysis and does not match against a CVE database. What it does is reason contextually about code patterns in the specific changes under review, flagging potential vulnerabilities in AI coverage of unsupported languages and frameworks where CodeQL has no built-in analysis. Results appear as the engine returns them rather than waiting for full CodeQL analysis to complete, and AI-generated alerts are labeled with an "AI" tag so developers can distinguish them from CodeQL's deterministic findings.
The two tools are designed to run in parallel, not in competition: the AI detection engine requires CodeQL default setup to be active on a repository in order to function, even though CodeQL is not performing the AI analysis itself. Disabling CodeQL disables the AI engine too.
The billing model reflects this LLM-based architecture. Unlike deterministic code scanning — where the computational cost is bounded by repository size and is included in GitHub Advanced Security licensing — AI Scan consumes credits under the Copilot AI credits billing model, drawing from an organization's pool only when detections actually run. The credit consumption model means the API's ability to control which repositories run AI Scan has direct cost implications at scale: organizations can contain credit spend by restricting AI Scan to their highest-priority repositories until they have confidence in the signal quality and detection rates.
Where AI Scan Sits in GitHub's Broader Security Architecture
The API release arrived in the middle of a concentrated period of security infrastructure updates from GitHub. The day before, September 9, GitHub announced that repository rulesets can now block pull requests exposing secrets — adding a hard enforcement gate at merge time that complements what earlier tools could only surface as warnings. Also on September 9, CodeQL 2.27.0 added ARM64 support, expanding the infrastructure surface on which deterministic analysis can run.
These updates form a coherent stack. The /security-review command in the Copilot CLI and desktop app catches vulnerabilities before a developer commits code. AI Scan and CodeQL catch vulnerabilities once a pull request is opened. The new PR secret-blocking rule prevents secrets from merging even if they reach the pull request stage. The AI Scan REST API lets security teams govern which repositories participate in the pull request detection layer, and at what pace.
Does GitHub Enterprise Server Support This?
No — and the timing of the exclusion is notable. GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22 reached GA on September 8, just two days before the AI Scan API announcement. The 3.22 release added Copilot CLI support for air-gapped environments and expanded enterprise team management capabilities, but it did not include AI Scan for pull requests or the new API endpoints. GitHub's changelog for the AI Scan API states explicitly that GitHub Enterprise Server is not supported in this release, with no roadmap date provided.
This exclusion affects a significant segment of enterprise GitHub customers. GitHub Enterprise Server is the self-hosted deployment option used by regulated industries — finance, healthcare, government, and defense contractors — where data-residency requirements, network-isolation mandates, or air-gapped operations make cloud hosting impractical or prohibited. Self-hosted GitHub Advanced Security customers on Server consistently receive new features one or more major releases later, as GitHub publishes to its cloud platform first and back-ports to Enterprise Server on a quarterly release cadence. The absence of AI Scan support from GHES 3.22 — released the same week as the API — signals that this particular gap may persist for several quarters.
Who Should Use This Preview Now
Enterprise organizations in the GitHub Advanced Security program are the relevant audience. The practical action during the preview window is to establish rollout scripts, calibrate false-positive rates against a representative selection of repositories, and wire AI Scan enablement and state data into existing vulnerability management workflows — Jira, ServiceNow, or internal security dashboards — before the API reaches general availability and locks into stable, versioned contracts.
GitHub has directed teams to the GitHub Community announcement thread (discussion #201543) for feedback during the preview period. The pace from the July feature preview to September API access — two months — suggests the team is iterating quickly, and general availability alongside eventual Enterprise Server support appears to be the logical roadmap target, even without a published commitment.
Frequently Asked Questions
What is GitHub AI Scan for pull requests, and how does it differ from CodeQL?
GitHub AI Scan is an LLM-based security detection engine that runs alongside CodeQL on pull requests and surfaces potential vulnerabilities in languages and frameworks that CodeQL's built-in analysis does not cover. Unlike CodeQL, which performs deterministic taint analysis using a semantic graph of the entire codebase, AI Scan uses probabilistic LLM inference on the specific code changes in a pull request. AI-generated findings are labeled with an "AI" tag to distinguish them from CodeQL results. The two tools are complementary: AI Scan requires CodeQL default setup to be active in order to function, and findings from AI Scan are informational rather than merge-blocking.
How do I enable AI scanning across all repositories in my GitHub organization?
The new API endpoints released on September 10, 2026 allow programmatic management of AI Scan enablement. Using the /orgs/{org}/code-scanning/ai-scan endpoint, an organization admin can enable AI Scan at the organization level through the REST API, replacing the previous requirement to configure each repository in the GitHub UI. Repository-level enablement can then be managed via /repos/{owner}/{repo}/code-scanning/ai-scan. Three prerequisites apply: an enterprise owner must allow AI security detections at the enterprise policy level, the organization must have GitHub Advanced Security enabled, and CodeQL default setup must be active on any repository targeted for AI scanning.
Does GitHub AI Scan work with GitHub Enterprise Server?
Not yet. GitHub's September 10 changelog explicitly states that GitHub Enterprise Server is not supported in this release. GitHub Enterprise Server 3.22, released September 8, did not include AI Scan or the new REST API endpoints. Organizations running self-hosted GitHub deployments for regulated-industry, air-gapped, or data-residency compliance reasons will need to wait for a future Enterprise Server release. No roadmap date has been announced.
What are AI credits in GitHub Copilot, and how does AI Scan consume them?
AI credits are GitHub's usage-based billing unit for Copilot's AI-powered capabilities. Unlike GitHub Advanced Security's deterministic code scanning — which is included in the GHAS license at a fixed cost — AI Scan draws down an organization's Copilot AI credit pool and consumes credits only when detections actually run. This variable-cost model means that using the new REST API to limit AI scanning to high-priority repositories is not only a security governance decision but also a cost management one: restricting AI Scan to the highest-risk repositories first contains credit spend while teams evaluate detection quality before broader rollout.
